The Government of Vietnam Proposes a Pilot Visa for Remote Workers

Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Lam Thi Phuong Thanh presented a draft resolution on special mechanisms and policies for tourism development to the National Assembly. The draft proposes a controlled pilot program for foreigners working remotely in Vietnam. It also includes more flexible visa and residency conditions for medical tourists and individuals coming for long-term treatment, rehabilitation, or relaxation, along with accompanying family members.

The proposal aims to attract higher-spending tourists and strengthen the competitiveness of the tourism industry. The draft includes the expansion of bilateral visa-free regimes for key markets and a more flexible visa policy prioritizing high-income, long-stay, and repeat visitors, as well as conference participants. The government also proposes simplifying the issuance of work permits, visas, and temporary residence for foreign experts and artists involved in tourism projects.

The pilot program for remote workers has not yet been adopted. The Culture and Social Affairs Committee of the National Assembly, while assessing the project, noted that the resolution should not establish specific visa rules for separate groups and called for further clarification on the novelty, features, and boundaries of the proposed special visa policy. Specific rules, fees, and application procedures for the pilot visa have not been established. Remote workers will continue to use the standard electronic visa valid for up to 90 days.

📌 Governance Snapshots: Why Your Tokens May Not Count in a DAO Vote

Main Points
⏺ Some DAOs calculate voting power using token balances from a specific blockchain block
⏺ Buying tokens after that snapshot may not increase your voting power
⏺ This post explains how balance snapshots work and why purchase timing matters

1️⃣ Core Idea — the protocol records balances at a selected block to determine how many votes each participant receives.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — a fixed reference point prevents voting power from changing every time tokens are transferred during the voting process.
3️⃣ Example — a vote uses balances from block #1000, but you buy tokens at block #1005. Those new tokens won't increase your voting power for that proposal.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — users may buy governance tokens specifically to participate, only to discover the snapshot already happened.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — before buying governance tokens, check the snapshot block, delegation conditions, and voting eligibility rules.

Final Thoughts

DAO governance isn't only about how many tokens you hold. It can also depend on when you held them. Sometimes your voting power is decided before the vote even begins.

April 15th, 1861, President Lincoln invoked the Insurrection Act to circumvent posse comitatus, in response to Fort Sumter. Then 12 days later, Lincoln unilaterally suspended the writ of habeas corpus while Congress was out of session (important), citing that he had to act immediately without Congressional approval, in order to suppress the rebellion and defend the public.

Then a few weeks later, in May 1861, a Circuit Court judge ruled that President Lincoln did not have the authority to suspend habeas corpus. Lincoln refused to comply with the ruling, and both he and the Military continued to do what was necessary. Lincoln then proceeded to do what he wanted without Congressional approval for almost two years, until Congress approved that he could suspend habeas corpus, whenever POTUS judged that public safety required it, and this stayed in effect throughout the war.

Lincoln pretty much told the judiciary to fuck off, and he told Congress that he had to act and could not wait for them, and honestly didn’t really need them. Lincoln was going to save the Republic during times of “rebellion or invasion”, and there wasn’t a damn thing anyone was going to do to stop him.

AIPAC’s Money Bought a Backlash

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), Washington’s leading pro-Israel lobby, entered electoral politics to make opposition to Israel costly. 

This year, Democratic candidates won votes by campaigning against AIPAC itself. Ties to the lobby became toxic, and its endorsement started to hurt the candidates it backed.


AIPAC’s super PAC, United Democracy Project, spent more than $50 million on the 2026 midterms through mid-October. 

Most of it went into Democratic primaries, though the lobby backs candidates in both parties and also spent to defeat Republican Rep. Thomas Massie in his primary. 

Weeks before the election, after a strategic review, AIPAC stopped endorsing candidates. It still runs the super PAC and now urges its donors to give directly to the candidates they favor. 

AIPAC says it helped 290 pro-Israel candidates win their elections and helped defeat 29 critics this year.

A new rival, American Priorities, spent roughly $8 million in Democratic primaries opposing military aid to Israel and backing sympathetic candidates. Unlike AIPAC, it does not support Republicans. 

Eleven incoming House members and two senators won their seats after primary campaigns it backed. 

The group said it wanted politicians to know that challenging AIPAC would bring money to their side. Its backing also opens a different donor network.

The backlash over Gaza is real, and American Priorities got results with a fraction of AIPAC’s money. But the machinery is familiar. Wealthy donors pick candidates, fund their campaigns, and expect a hearing afterward.

In Democratic primaries, AIPAC no longer holds a monopoly on the threat of a well-funded challenge. Democrats in Congress now have a choice of sponsors.

👀 Justin Sun becomes PEPE’s largest individual holder, Arkham says 

🌐 Tron founder Justin Sun has accumulated nearly 3% of PEPE’s supply, with blockchain analytics firm Arkham Intelligence identifying approximately $51.25 million worth of the memecoin across his known and suspected wallets. According to an October 27 Arkham Intelligence report, the tokens entered Sun-linked wallets over the previous 10 days, making him the largest individual PEPE holder outside cryptocurrency exchanges.

🔗 The firm estimated his combined holdings at 2.82% of PEPE’s supply, although some wallets included in its calculations were attributed to Sun through blockchain analysis. At the time, PEPE had a market capitalization of approximately $1.81 billion, with exchanges controlling several of the largest known holdings.

📊 Binance held $337.5 million worth of PEPE, representing 18.7% of the supply, followed by Robinhood with $150.9 million, or 8.37%. Coinbase and OKX accounted for another 5.03% and 4.15%, respectively. Unlike Sun’s attributed holdings, exchange balances generally include assets held on behalf of customers, meaning their large positions do not necessarily represent investments made by the platforms themselves.
